Managing Negative Press: How to Respond to a Critical Article in Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Negative press management starts with a cool assessment of what the article actually says, followed by the right tool: a correction under the Italian press law when facts are wrong, a private conversation with the journalist when context is missing, or deliberate silence when any reaction would only extend the story. Removal is rarely the first move with a fresh article, but the steps you take in the first days decide which options remain open later.

Assess the article before you react

The first task is to separate factual errors from unfavourable but accurate reporting, because each calls for a different response and confusing them is the most common mistake companies make. An article can be painful without being false, and a factual error can be minor even in a hostile piece.

Read the text with your legal and communications advisers and answer a few questions in writing:

  • Which statements are verifiably false, and which documents prove it?
  • Which statements are opinions, interpretations or quotes from third parties?
  • Was your company asked for comment before publication, and was its position reported fairly?
  • How large and relevant is the audience: a national daily, a local Milan or Rome outlet, a trade publication?
  • Is the story already being picked up by aggregators, social accounts or other newsrooms?

This note becomes the reference for every later decision and prevents the reaction from being driven by the anger of the first hour.

Using the right of reply under the Italian press law

When an article attributes to you facts, actions or statements you consider false or damaging, article 8 of the Italian press law (Legge 8 febbraio 1948, n. 47) gives you the right to a correction, known as rettifica. The editor-in-chief must publish it free of charge, with the same prominence as the original article, provided the text is not itself of criminal relevance.

For daily newspapers the correction must appear within two days of receiving the request; periodicals have a slightly longer window tied to their publication schedule. If the editor refuses or ignores the request, you can apply to the court for an order requiring publication. Registered online newspapers are generally expected to honour the same principle, and in practice most Italian online newsrooms handle correction requests in a similar way.

  1. Address the request to the editor-in-chief (direttore responsabile) by certified email (PEC) or registered letter.
  2. Identify the article precisely: title, date, page or URL.
  3. Quote each contested statement and state the correct facts briefly, without insults or commentary.
  4. Keep the text within the length limit set by the law, which is thirty lines.
  5. Attach supporting documents to the cover letter, not to the text intended for publication.

A rettifica corrects facts; it is not a platform for a counter-attack. A sober correction is published as written, while a polemical one invites refusal and a second round of coverage.

Working with the journalist and the editor

A direct, private contact with the journalist is often more effective than a formal request, especially when the problem is missing context rather than a clear falsehood. Journalists in Italy, as elsewhere, care about accuracy and about their relationship with sources; a well-documented call or email can lead to an update of the online version or a note at the bottom of the piece within hours.

Offer facts, documents and a named spokesperson available for questions. Avoid legal threats in the first contact, requests to "take the article down" and any attempt to involve advertising relationships, all of which tend to end up in the next article. If the newsroom agrees to update the text, ask for a visible update note rather than a silent edit, because readers and other journalists then see that the original version was corrected.

When staying silent is the better strategy

Silence is the right choice when the article is accurate, the audience is limited and the story has no obvious next chapter. A press release, a public rebuttal on social media or a lawsuit announced to the press can turn a single article read by a few thousand people into negative media coverage across several outlets.

Every public reaction is a new news hook. Before responding, ask whether your statement gives journalists a reason to write a second article.

Staying silent publicly does not mean doing nothing. Prepare a short holding statement for customers, employees and partners who ask, brief your front-line staff, and make sure your own channels answer the question calmly for anyone who searches for it.

Handling follow-up coverage and syndication

A single article in Italy is frequently copied by regional sites, aggregators and blogs within days, sometimes without the later correction or update. Monitoring your brand name and the key phrases of the story lets you identify each copy early and decide whether it needs action.

When a copy repeats a statement already corrected, send the publisher the rettifica or the update with a short request to align the text. If the story concerns proceedings that later end in your favour, such as an investigation archived or a dispute settled, ask the original outlet to publish the outcome. Newsrooms are generally more willing to add an update than to remove an article, and an updated article is far less damaging in search results than a stale one.

When negative press removal becomes realistic

Negative press removal is realistic in two situations: when the article is defamatory, and when time has made it irrelevant. A false and damaging article can support a defamation claim or an urgent court order, while an accurate article may become eligible for delisting years later under the right to be forgotten, as explained in our guide on what can really be removed from Google.

Between those two points, most companies combine corrections and updates with positive owned content, so that a critical article no longer dominates the first page; the trade-offs between these approaches are set out in removal, deindexing and suppression compared.
